result: Depletion of caveolin-1 and cavin-1 increases TEM formation frequency. siRNA-mediated knockdown of caveolin-1 (siCAV1) and cavin-1 (siPTRF) both increase the percentage of cells displaying TEMs and the density of TEMs per cell. RhoA inhibition by ExoC3 reduces caveolae density at the plasma membrane by 1.6-fold, and the remaining caveolae are evenly distributed without accumulation around TEMs.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, stating 'This important study identifies the role of caveolin-1 and cavin1 as regulators of transendothelial macroaperture (TEM)' and describe the work as 'rigorous and compelling.' The reviewer notes 'the accumulation of pieces of evidence collected from each type of approach makes very convincing the conclusion drawn by the authors.'

result: Caveolae depletion and RhoA inhibition synergistically reduce cell height to favor TEM nucleation. Depletion of caveolin-1 and cavin-1 decreases cell volume and increases cell spreading, which together reduce cell height. This reduction in cell height, combined with disruption of the F-actin meshwork by RhoA inhibition, favors membrane apposition required for TEM nucleation.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without critique. The reviewer specifically praises the 'quality of STORM images (Fig. 2) which are very illuminating and useful, in particular for validating some hypotheses of the theoretical analysis,' directly supporting the actin meshwork observations. The comprehensive nature of the work is noted as making the conclusions 'very convincing.'

result: Caveolin-1 specifically controls TEM opening speed and maximal width. TEMs are 5.4-fold wider in siCAV1-treated cells compared to controls, with a twofold higher opening speed (2.4 µm²/s vs 1.1 µm²/s). In contrast, cavin-1 depletion has only minor effects on TEM opening dynamics, while the time to reach maximal diameter remains identical across all conditions.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm this as a key finding, stating the work 'pins down the key role of caveolin-1' and noting that the evidence makes 'very convincing the conclusion drawn by the authors on the new role of cavolin-1 as an individual protein instead of the main molecular component of caveolae.' The distinction between caveolin-1 and cavin-1 effects is implicitly accepted through the overall positive assessment.

result: Caveolin-1 deficiency sensitizes mice to lethal effects of EDIN-B during S. aureus bloodstream infection. CAV1 KO mice show significantly higher lethality when infected with S. aureus producing catalytically active EDIN-B compared to the inactive mutant or deletion strain. This establishes that caveolin-1 expression confers resistance to EDIN-B mART pathogenicity during septicemia.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this in vivo validation, describing the work as 'comprehensive' with 'in vitro work based on siRNA knockdown and optical imaging approach complemented with an in vivo work on mice.' The multi-faceted approach including mouse experiments is noted as contributing to the 'very convincing' nature of the conclusions.

result: Caveolin-1 specifically increases membrane bending rigidity independent of caveolae. Membrane tether pulling experiments show caveolin-1 depletion decreases bending rigidity by 30% (from 23.4 to 17.0 kBT), while cavin-1 depletion has no effect. Theoretical modeling predicts a 55% reduction, with the difference attributed to model approximations. Caveolin-1 depletion also increases membrane tension twofold, while cavin-1 depletion affects neither tension nor rigidity.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding, stating 'the accumulation of pieces of evidence collected from each type of approach makes very convincing the conclusion drawn by the authors on the new role of cavolin-1 as an individual protein.' The biophysical measurements are part of the 'rigorous' methodology that is 'compelling.' The theoretical modeling is discussed positively below.

result: Membrane tension and bending rigidity are the minimal mechanical parameters determining TEM nucleation and maximal size. The theoretical model based on dewetting processes predicts that membrane rigidity sets maximal TEM aperture size, and that the minimal precursor tunnel size increases with bending rigidity and decreases with membrane tension. The model shows reasonable agreement with experimental measurements despite some approximations.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly validate the theoretical approach, stating 'The analogy with dewetting processes drawn to derive the theoretical model is very attractive' and noting that 'the STORM analysis...show that HUVECs intoxicated by ExoC3 exhibit a loose and defective cortex with a significantly increase mesh size, which supports this hypothesis.' The reviewer acknowledges that 'the validity of the Helfrich formalism is a key assumption' but accepts it is now supported by the STORM data.

result: The mechanism by which caveolin-1 increases membrane rigidity remains uncertain. The authors discuss several hypotheses including direct mechanical effects of caveolin-1 insertion, indirect effects through lipid composition changes (cholesterol, sphingomyelin, glycosphingolipids enrichment), but acknowledge the exact mechanism requires further investigation. Previous studies suggest protein inclusions typically soften rather than stiffen membranes.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this limitation, stating 'While this work pins down the key role of caveolin-1, its mechanism remains to be further investigated' and 'Even though we may feel slightly frustrated by the absence of data in this direction, the quality and merit of this paper remain.' The hypotheses are described as 'very plausible though challenging.'

result: Background and contextual claims about endothelial barrier function, bacterial toxins, caveolae structure, and related literature. These claims establish the scientific context including: mART exotoxins compromise endothelial barriers by inhibiting RhoA; caveolae are mechano-regulators that buffer membrane tension; caveolin-1 and RhoA crosstalk is important for endothelial mechanosensing; and variations in caveolin-1 expression have bidirectional impacts on S. aureus susceptibility.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question these background claims, which are well-supported by citations and represent established knowledge in the field. The reviewers focus their evaluation on the novel experimental findings rather than the contextual framework.
